subject: Business Models
title: eToys: Holiday Meltdown
description: A fast breakdown of eToys: Holiday Meltdown for builders.

hook.text: eToys IPO'd at $78/share in 1999, briefly worth more than Toys R Us. It was bankrupt by February 2001.

buildup.text: eToys spent heavily on holiday marketing to compete with Toys R Us for Christmas shoppers.

discovery.text: The 1999 Christmas rush overwhelmed its logistics. Toys arrived late. Furious parents flooded customer support.

twist.text: eToys' customer acquisition cost was $150 per buyer. The average customer spent $105. It lost money per sale.

climax.text: Seasonal businesses need perfect execution during peak. One bad Christmas can destroy years of brand building.

punchline.text: Worth more than Toys R Us. Dead 14 months later. One bad Christmas was fatal.

quiz.question: Why did eToys fail despite high valuation?
options: Customer acquisition cost exceeded customer spending

details.summary: eToys.com reached a market cap exceeding Toys R Us despite a fraction of the revenue, then collapsed when holiday 2000 overwhelmed its logistics. Orders arrived late or not at all, destroying customer trust. The company filed for bankruptcy in 2001 with just 30 million in annual revenue.
details.whyItMatters: eToys proves that a soaring stock price and massive brand awareness mean nothing if the operational backbone cannot deliver the product. Logistics capability must scale alongside marketing and customer acquisition.
takeaways: Market cap exceeded Toys R Us despite tiny revenue during the dot-com bubble
Holiday logistics failure destroyed customer trust and repeat business
Operational capability must match marketing reach and customer expectations

faq.question: How did eToys reach a higher market cap than Toys R Us?
faq.answer: Dot-com era investors valued growth potential over current revenue. eToys had a compelling e-commerce narrative and rapid customer acquisition. At peak, its market cap was 8 billion dollars on 30 million in annual revenue, a P/S ratio of over 250 times.

faq.question: What specifically went wrong with eToys' holiday logistics?
faq.answer: The company underestimated holiday order volume and overpromised delivery dates. Warehouse systems could not handle the surge. Shipping partnerships failed to scale. Thousands of orders arrived after Christmas or not at all, generating massive customer complaints and refund requests.
